summary: Baimix Live Holdings, LLC (client, Buyer) acquired the regional concert promotion and festival business of Tinev Concerts & Festivals, Inc. (Seller) under an Asset Purchase Agreement that signed and closed on January 12, 2026. The purchase price was $30,000,000: cash at closing, a $3,000,000 indemnity escrow, and a $6,000,000 Seller Note issued by Buyer. The folder holds the APA, the superseded LOI, the Escrow Agreement, the Key Employee Agreement with Seller's head of talent booking, the Seller Note, and a post-closing Letter Agreement dated October 6, 2026. Two distractors are included: a stage lighting rental agreement and Seller's closing officer's certificate. Five issues are planted. (1) Read with the APA's uncapped Buyer indemnity, the APA's definition of Assumed Liabilities makes Buyer answer without limit for Seller's pre-closing contract liabilities, contrary to the LOI. (2) The Letter Agreement narrows 'Fundamental Representations', which pulls title claims under the APA cap. (3) Buyer's July 20, 2026 claim notice missed the escrow release date and was not sent to the Escrow Agent. (4) A sale of Buyer to Orrant Media Partners, recited in the Letter Agreement, triggers the Seller Note's change-of-control consent default. (5) The Seller Note chooses California law and Los Angeles courts, against the APA's New York law and forum, and the APA's precedence clause lets the note control.

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: APA Section 2.3(a) defines Assumed Liabilities to include all Liabilities under the Assigned Contracts (artist engagement, venue booking and sponsorship contracts) 'whether arising prior to, on or after the Closing Date'. APA Section 9.3(b) requires Buyer to indemnify Seller for all Losses arising from Assumed Liabilities. APA Section 9.5 states that claims under Section 9.3(b) 'shall not be subject to the Cap' or the basket. Read together, these provisions make Buyer liable without limit for Seller's own pre-closing breaches of the assigned contracts, such as unpaid artist guarantees or pre-closing venue damage claims, and Buyer must indemnify Seller for them. This departs from the LOI (D2 Section 3), under which Buyer would assume only post-closing contract liabilities. The LOI is superseded, so it shows the agreed deal but does not cure the APA.
detect_terms: whether arising prior to, on or after the Closing Date
shall not be subject to the Cap
issues.expected_finding: Because Section 2.3(a) sweeps pre-closing liabilities under the Assigned Contracts into Assumed Liabilities and Sections 9.3(b) and 9.5 make Buyer's indemnity for Assumed Liabilities uncapped, Buyer bears unlimited exposure for Seller's pre-closing contract breaches contrary to the LOI's post-closing-only assumption, and the definition should be amended to limit Assumed Liabilities to obligations arising after the Closing Date.

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description: Under APA Section 9.5(a), Seller's liability for representation breaches is capped at $3,600,000, but the Cap does not apply to Losses from breach of Fundamental Representations. APA Section 1.1 defines Fundamental Representations as Sections 4.1 (Organization), 4.2 (Authority), 4.7 (Title to Purchased Assets, covering the festival brand, trademarks and ticketing database) and 4.19 (Brokers), and Section 9.1 gives them a six-year survival period. Section 3 of the October 6, 2026 Letter Agreement (D6), presented as a conforming clarification, restates the definition as 'Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.19', which silently drops Section 4.7. APA Section 11.11 ranks signed letter agreements first, so the narrower definition controls. Title and IP ownership claims, the most valuable protection for an asset buyer, now fall under the $3,600,000 Cap and, as general representations, survive only 18 months. Neither document alone shows this: the APA carve-out is favourable to Buyer, and the letter's definition looks like a routine restatement.
issues.expected_finding: The Letter Agreement's restated definition of Fundamental Representations omits Section 4.7 and, because signed letter agreements prevail under APA Section 11.11, removes title to the Purchased Assets from the Section 9.5(a) carve-out so Buyer's title and IP claims are now capped at $3,600,000 (and survive only 18 months), and Buyer should seek to reinstate Section 4.7 by further amendment.

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description: Escrow Agreement (D3) Section 4.2 sets the Release Date at six months following the Closing Date of January 12, 2026, which is July 12, 2026. On that date the Escrow Agent releases the $3,000,000 Escrow Funds to Seller, except amounts covered by Claim Notices delivered to the Escrow Agent before the Release Date. Recital B of the October 6, 2026 Letter Agreement (D6) records that Buyer delivered its indemnification claim notice, dated July 20, 2026, to Seller only, asserting $1,150,000 of Losses for breach of the sponsorship contracts representation in Section 4.11. The notice therefore came after the Release Date and never reached the Escrow Agent. Under APA Section 11.11 the Escrow Agreement controls as to escrow release, so the 18-month APA survival period does not extend the escrow. The same recital records that Seller disputes the claim and that each party reserves all rights, so Buyer has not accepted loss of the claim. Neither document alone shows the lapse.
detect_terms: six (6) months following the Closing Date
delivered to Escrow Agent prior to the Release Date
issues.expected_finding: Buyer's July 20, 2026 claim notice was delivered after the July 12, 2026 Release Date and not to the Escrow Agent, so the escrow could be released to Seller and Buyer's $1,150,000 claim, though still timely under the APA's 18-month survival period, is unsecured; Buyer should pursue Seller directly, consider setoff against the Seller Note, and seek Seller's agreement to re-escrow the disputed amount.

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: Seller Note (D5) Section 6.1(g) makes it an Event of Default if Maker undergoes a Change of Control without the prior written consent of Holder. On an Event of Default, Holder may accelerate the unpaid principal of the $6,000,000 note under Section 6.2. Change of Control is defined to include any Person other than Baimix Group Holdings, Inc. acquiring, directly or indirectly, more than 50% of Maker's equity. Recital D of the October 6, 2026 Letter Agreement (D6) records that Baimix Group Holdings, Inc. entered into a Membership Interest Purchase Agreement dated September 22, 2026 to sell all membership interests of Buyer to Orrant Media Partners, L.P., with closing expected in December 2026. The Letter Agreement contains no consent from Seller, and no other document in the folder does either. Read together, the pending sale will trigger a default and acceleration right in Seller's favour unless Seller consents. Each half reads as ordinary on its own.
issues.expected_finding: The pending sale of Buyer to Orrant Media Partners recited in the Letter Agreement is a Change of Control under Seller Note Section 6.1(g), so absent Seller's prior written consent, which has not been obtained, it will be an Event of Default allowing Seller to accelerate the $6,000,000 note, and Buyer must obtain Seller's written consent or arrange repayment before that sale closes.

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: Seller Note (D5) Section 10 chooses the laws of the State of California and submits all disputes under the note to the exclusive jurisdiction of courts in the County of Los Angeles. APA (D1) Section 11.8 chooses New York law and requires disputes arising out of the APA 'or any Ancillary Agreement' (which includes the Seller Note) to be brought exclusively in courts in the County of New York. APA Section 11.11 provides that each Ancillary Agreement controls as to its own subject matter, so the note's California clause governs note disputes. The note's setoff right (Section 5) depends on indemnity claims determined under the APA. Seller can therefore sue for note payments in Los Angeles under California law while Buyer's indemnity claims, including the July 20, 2026 claim, must be litigated in New York under New York law. This creates duplicative proceedings and a risk of inconsistent rulings on setoff. Each forum clause is ordinary on its own; the conflict appears only when both are read with Section 11.11.
detect_terms: laws of the State of California
issues.expected_finding: The Seller Note's California law and exclusive Los Angeles forum conflict with the APA's New York law and exclusive New York County forum for Ancillary Agreements, and because APA Section 11.11 lets the note control its own subject matter, Buyer's setoff and indemnity disputes would be split across two forums and two laws, so the note should be amended to adopt New York law and the New York forum.
